summary: For ages 9–11, resolve the rainforest nutrient paradox: the lushest forests on Earth typically grow on thin, nutrient-poor soil because most nutrients are stored in living biomass rather than the ground. Warm, wet conditions drive rapid decomposition, and much of the released nutrient is quickly reabsorbed by shallow roots and mycorrhizal fungi in a fast, nearly closed loop. Clearing the forest removes much of the nutrient store and breaks the loop, so cleared farmland often gives good crops at first but declines within a few years unless nutrients are added. Learners run and break the loop, trace where nutrients actually sit, and contrast rainforest with temperate soil.
misconceptions: 'Lush growth means rich, deep soil' — rainforest soil is actually thin and nutrient-poor.
'Nutrients sit in the soil waiting' — they are locked in living things and recycled almost instantly.
'Cleared rainforest makes great long-term farmland' — it yields briefly then fails once the nutrient bank is gone.
'Decomposition is slow like a compost heap' — in warm, wet conditions it is very rapid.
'Rain helps fertilise the soil' — on bare ground heavy rain leaches nutrients away (only the fast loop retains them).

activities.title: Run and break the nutrient loop
steps: Predict first: 'The richest forest on Earth grows on some of the poorest soil — how can that be?' Write down your guess about where the nutrients are before investigating.

Trace the loop stage by stage: a leaf falls → warm, wet conditions speed up decomposers (fungi, bacteria, insects) → nutrients are released → shallow surface roots and fungal partners (mycorrhizae) quickly absorb most of them, before rain can wash much away.
Track where the nutrients are at each stage using a 'mostly here / less here' split: most of the available nutrients in the living biomass (trees and plants), relatively little in the soil.
Increase warmth and moisture and observe how much faster decomposition and re-uptake happen; compare with a cool British wood where it is slow.

Now break the loop: clear the forest. In the model, see that much of the nutrient store is removed or lost with the trees, rain leaches the bare soil, and a farm plot without added fertiliser gives a good crop at first, then poorer ones, then fails after a few years.
State the resolution in your own words: the forest is rich because the forest itself is the main storehouse; the thin soil beneath was never the main store.
activities.insight: The nutrient 'bank' of a rainforest is held mostly in the living biomass and recycled rapidly through a nearly closed loop, not stored in rich deep soil — so removing the trees removes much of the nutrient store and breaks the loop, which is why cleared farmland often declines within a few years unless nutrients are added.

activities.title: Label the loop on a forest cross-section
steps: Examine a forest cross-section and identify each stage in turn: the fallen leaf litter, the fungi and insect decomposers, the shallow surface roots, and the thin soil layer beneath.
For each part, say what it does in the loop and describe how it connects to the next stage.
Use a flap or split labelled 'nutrients here (biomass)' versus 'not here (soil)' to mark where the nutrient store really sits.
Explain in a sentence why the roots are shallow and why the fungal partners matter for grabbing nutrients quickly.
activities.insight: Each physical layer of the rainforest plays a specific role in a continuous, fast recycling loop, and the nutrient store is in the living layers, not the soil.

activities.title: Sequence the loop and explain the farm failure
steps: Put the decomposition loop in order: dead material → decomposers → nutrients released → absorbed by roots/fungi → new growth.
Answer and justify: why does cleared rainforest farmland fail after only a few years? Give the reason, not just the fact.

Respond to the diagnostic scenario: 'A rainforest grows the lushest plant life on Earth. A farmer thinks the soil must be amazingly rich, clears a patch, farms it, but within a few years the crops fail. Why does the richest-looking forest sit on poor soil, and why does the farm fail?'
Tackle the stretch question: if the cleared nutrients could somehow be kept in the soil, would the farm still fail? Explain your reasoning.
activities.insight: Ordering the loop and explaining the failure requires connecting three ideas — nutrients in biomass, rapid recycling, and clearing breaking the loop — rather than just recalling that the soil is poor.

activities.title: Contrast rainforest with a temperate forest
steps: Compare two soil-depth cross-sections: a thin rainforest surface layer versus a deep temperate-forest soil layer.

Explain where the nutrients are stored in each: mostly in biomass with fast recycling in the rainforest, versus a much larger share stored in the leaf litter and deep soil in the cooler temperate forest.
Predict what happens to farmland after clearing in each case, and explain why the outcomes differ.
activities.insight: Comparing a biomass-store forest with a deep-soil-store forest sharpens the central idea that it is where nutrients are kept, not how lush the growth looks, that determines whether cleared land stays fertile.

checkQuestion: A rainforest grows the lushest, densest plant life on Earth. A farmer thinks: 'that soil must be amazingly rich — perfect for crops.' They clear a patch and farm it, but within a few years the crops fail. Why does the richest-looking forest sit on poor soil, and WHY does the farm fail?
checkAnswer: The soil itself is thin and nutrient-poor — nearly all the nutrients are locked up in the living plants and trees, not in the ground. In the warm, wet forest, dead material is broken down very fast by decomposers and the released nutrients are grabbed straight back by roots and fungi (a rapid closed loop), so little stays in the soil. Clearing the forest removes that store of nutrients (the biomass) and the loop; the thin soil is quickly exhausted and washed out by rain, so the farm fails after a few years.
